hook.text: In 1943, Mexico imported half its wheat. By 1964, it was a net exporter. One research program did that.

buildup.text: The Rockefeller Foundation partnered with Mexico's government to fund Borlaug's wheat breeding program.

discovery.text: Borlaug's rust-resistant, high-yield varieties spread across Mexican farms. Yields tripled in 20 years.

twist.text: Success in Mexico proved the model worked. It became the template for India, Pakistan, and beyond.

climax.text: The Mexican program became CIMMYT—a global center that still breeds wheat and corn for the developing world.

punchline.text: Mexico was the laboratory. The world was the patient.

quiz.question: What institution grew out of Mexico's wheat breeding program?
options: CIMMYT—the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center

details.summary: Mexico was the birthplace of the Green Revolution, where Borlaug began his wheat breeding work in 1944. By 1963, Mexico had transformed from a wheat importer to a net exporter, demonstrating that science could solve developing-world food crises and inspiring global replication.
details.whyItMatters: Mexico's success served as the proof of concept for the entire Green Revolution. The Rockefeller Foundation's Mexican Agricultural Program showed that targeted investment in crop breeding could transform a nation's food production within two decades.
takeaways: Mexico's wheat yields increased sixfold between 1944 and 1963 with Borlaug's varieties
Mexico went from importing half its wheat to becoming a net wheat exporter
The Mexican success convinced donors and governments to fund similar programs worldwide

faq.question: How did the Green Revolution begin in Mexico?
faq.answer: In 1943, the Rockefeller Foundation partnered with the Mexican government to improve agricultural production. Norman Borlaug was hired in 1944 to breed disease-resistant, high-yielding wheat.

faq.question: Why did Mexico serve as the model for the Green Revolution?
faq.answer: Mexico demonstrated the complete package: new varieties, fertilizer, irrigation, and farmer education could transform a food-deficit nation into a food exporter. This proof of concept convinced the Rockefeller and Ford Foundations to fund similar programs in India, Pakistan, and the Philippines.
